name: Japanese
notes: Start with hiragana — it is a true alphabet of 46 sounds and can be learned in a week. Once you can read it, everything else in Japanese becomes approachable. Japanese has no tones and very regular pronunciation, which makes speaking it far easier than reading it.
syllabus: Both kana in full, 110 kanji (the whole JLPT N5 kanji list), and about 590 words and phrases — roughly three-quarters of N5 vocabulary (around 800 words). N5 is the first of five official levels; passing it means simple, slow conversations. Grammar is in the sentence-patterns deck and the guide. Cards can be spoken aloud if Windows has a Japanese voice installed. Still missing: the last of the N5 words, and N4.
